questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: Which Explanation an Approach Treats as Central
questions.learningObjective: identify the level of explanation a personality approach takes to be primary
questions.stem: One researcher spends her career ranking people on a small number of stable dimensions, while another spends hers reconstructing early childhood from what a client reports about a present difficulty. Which pair of approaches is at work?

options.text: Trait and psychodynamic, since the first treats measured dispositions as primary and the second treats early experience as primary
Behavioural and trait, since the first builds its account from observed frequency and the second from observed consistency
options.misconception: swaps a reconstruction of early experience for a tally of observable acts

options.text: Humanistic and trait, since the first takes a person's own account of themselves as primary and the second takes measured dispositions
options.misconception: recasts a reconstruction of early experience as a humanistic appeal to self-report

options.text: Social-cognitive and psychodynamic, since the first treats mutual shaping as primary and the second treats early experience as primary
options.misconception: reads a ranking of stable dimensions as an account of mutual shaping

questions.explanation: Approaches to personality differ most plainly in what they nominate as the thing that needs explaining. A trait account puts the stable disposition first, so the research question is how consistently people can be ordered on a dimension, and the childhood material would count as one possible source of the ordering rather than as the explanation itself. A psychodynamic account puts early experience first, so the present difficulty is the surface of the account and the reconstruction of what happened before is the substance, and a ranking would be evidence only of ordering, not of cause. The behavioural option fails because counting how often a response appears describes a rate, not a reconstruction, and nothing in the case involves one. The humanistic option fails because a client reporting their own experience as trustworthy is a claim about the value of self-report, and the first researcher is not making that claim. The social-cognitive option fails because mutual shaping names a reciprocal process between person and setting, and ranking people on a scale says nothing about any process at all.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two researchers is explaining the person and which is explaining the person's history.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: Evidence a Psychodynamic Account Would Count as Support
questions.learningObjective: identify the kind of result a psychodynamic account treats as its strongest support
questions.stem: A clinician argues that a client's difficulty trusting colleagues repeats an unresolved early relationship, and the pattern first shows up in sessions about childhood. Which result would that account treat as its strongest support?

options.text: A recurring theme that is already present in the account before the present difficulty is discussed, and returns whenever it is avoided
A validated inventory score that rises when the client is asked to rate how much childhood difficulty they recall
options.misconception: treats a questionnaire score as the kind of evidence a case reconstruction can build on

options.text: A controlled comparison in which people with closely matched scores respond differently to the same situation
options.misconception: offers a group comparison as the decisive support for a reading of one client's history

options.text: A treatment outcome in which the inventory score falls after the early relationship has been discussed at length
options.misconception: counts a score that moves with the demand of the session as independent confirmation

questions.explanation: A psychodynamic account is built from a single case read in depth, so it takes its support from the internal structure of that case rather than from a score or a comparison group. A theme that appears before the presenting difficulty is named, and returns when the person steers away from it, is the kind of ordering an account of repetition needs, because repetition is a claim about sequence and sequence is what the account rests on. The inventory option fails because a score that moves when a topic is raised is what any account of a state-dependent kind of material would produce, and it moves for reasons that include the demand of the question itself. The comparison option fails because matched scores responding differently is evidence about the limits of scores rather than about an early relationship, and it is the kind of result a trait account finds congenial. The treatment option fails because a fall in a score after talking about the past is exactly the pattern a self-report account predicts from the demand of the session, so it cannot separate the accounts that matter.
questions.hint: Ask whether the result is a quality of this one case, or a number that a comparison group could also produce.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: An Object That Carries a Family Memory
questions.learningObjective: identify the role an object plays in a psychodynamic interview
questions.stem: In a first session a client is asked to talk about anything that comes to mind while holding an old hammer whose handle has been replaced twice. The client speaks at length about how careful the family always had to be with things that could be broken. What is the hammer doing in this account?

options.text: Acting as a prompt for a displaced theme, letting material about the family surface without being asked about directly
Acting as a steadying control, holding the client's attention to the object so that drift between sessions is reduced
options.misconception: invents a control comparison the session as described does not contain

options.text: Testing a sensory preference, so that the client's handling of the object reveals a stable perceptual style
options.misconception: reads an object chosen for its family history as a probe of sensory style

options.text: Dating the recall, since the replaced handle fixes the event to one period of the client's childhood
options.misconception: mistakes a twice-repaired handle for a precise record of when an event occurred

questions.explanation: The case is built the way these accounts are usually built, with an object chosen because it touches a history rather than because it measures anything, and what makes it diagnostic is where the talk goes. The client begins from the object and arrives at a family rule about breakage, and neither the object nor the rule was the assigned topic, which is the shape an account of displaced attention takes. The control option fails because no comparison is running, since nothing in the vignette pairs this object with a neutral one or varies anything between sessions, so no control is in evidence. The sensory option fails because the client's talk is about a family rule and not about how the object feels to hold, and the handle is described rather than reacted to. The dating option fails because a replaced handle identifies no particular year and in any case the account is about a repeated pattern rather than a located event.
questions.hint: Ask what the object is for in the account: what it is made to do, and what the talk that followed it shows.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: What a Person-Centred Approach Says a Therapist Is For
questions.learningObjective: state the therapist's role in a person-centred account
questions.stem: A person-centred therapist tells a client that the client's own sense of what is real counts for more than the therapist's judgement of progress. What is the therapist supplying, in that account?

options.text: A relationship in which the client's experience is treated as trustworthy, so the material can be explored without being argued with
A method for correcting the client's distorted view of events, so that later judgements are more accurate than the first ones
options.misconception: puts the therapist in the business of overruling the client's own account

options.text: A programme of exercises chosen for the client's condition, so that the desired change is produced reliably and on schedule
options.misconception: assumes a diagnosis and a planned course of treatment, which the account sets aside

options.text: A standard of the ideal self, so the client can measure the distance between how things are and how they should be
options.misconception: makes the therapist's picture of a better self the yardstick the client is measured against

questions.explanation: The position in the vignette is the defining commitment of a person-centred account, and its consequence is about what may and may not be done inside the session. If the client's own frame is the trustworthy one, then the therapist's part is to provide a relationship in which that frame can be examined without being challenged, which is why a value such as unconditional positive regard appears in the same accounts. The correction option fails because improving accuracy means overriding the client's frame, which is precisely what the account declines to do, and a distortion is assumed only from outside the frame. The programme option fails because it puts the design of the change in the therapist's hands and treats the condition as something given, and a person-centred account refuses the first and does not diagnose in the second. The standard option fails because an ideal self is the therapist's picture, and the account inverts exactly that by putting the client's own picture first.
questions.hint: Ask what follows for the therapist's role once the client's own frame is taken as the reliable one.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: What Reciprocal Determination Adds to a Learning Account
questions.learningObjective: explain what reciprocal determinism changes about where causal control sits
questions.stem: A learning account of personality says conduct is shaped by its consequences. A social-cognitive account adds that person, behaviour and environment pull on each other. What does the addition change about where control sits?

options.text: It makes the direction of influence circular, so a person can change a setting and a setting can change what the person does next
It fixes the direction of influence on the environment, since situations become the only active cause in the scheme
options.misconception: makes the environment the sole active cause, which is the opposite of a reciprocal scheme

options.text: It removes the part played by consequences, since past reinforcement stops predicting how strong a response is
options.misconception: concludes that consequences stop mattering, which no part of the addition states

options.text: It treats the three factors as independent, so each can be varied without disturbing the other two in the design
options.misconception: denies mutual influence while claiming a scheme in which each part acts on the others

questions.explanation: The addition is worth isolating because it is small in wording and large in consequence. A consequence-based account has a direction, the environment acts and the behaviour responds, which makes it straightforward to design a study. Reciprocal determinism removes the fixed direction and closes the loop, so the person is at once an outcome of earlier settings and a cause of later ones, and the same person can be an easy setting for one task and a hard one for the next. The environment option fails because it keeps the environment causal but makes it the only cause, which is the opposite of what a circular scheme says. The consequences option fails because nothing in the addition withdraws reinforcement, and a reading in which consequences stop mattering would be a different theory rather than an extension of this one. The independence option fails because mutual influence is precisely the denial of independence, and it also makes the account very hard to test, since three things cannot be varied one at a time without disturbing the others.
questions.hint: Ask whether the account still has a direction in which causes run from one term to another.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: Claims About the Main Approaches
questions.learningObjective: judge which claims about approaches to personality are supported
questions.stem: Four claims about approaches to personality are offered. Which two of them are supported? Select both.

options.text: A trait account can describe a person accurately while saying nothing about how the description came to be true
Two approaches can disagree about one person's conduct and both be working from the evidence they regard as good
A psychodynamic account is refuted as soon as a client's account of childhood proves to be factually wrong
options.misconception: believes these accounts treat the client's recollection as a report to be audited

options.text: The behavioural and social-cognitive approaches differ only in vocabulary, since both make reward the operative variable
options.misconception: assumes an account built on reciprocal influence can be reduced to reinforcement terms

questions.explanation: The first supported claim separates two things that are often run together, description and explanation, and a trait inventory is a description by design, since it locates a person on a scale without asserting anything about origin. A description can be accurate and leave the causal question untouched, which is why a trait account can be empirically respectable and still be accused of explaining nothing. The second supported claim says the approaches differ in what counts as evidence, and a behavioural account and a psychodynamic one can look at the same recorded session and weight it differently without either of them being careless. The third option fails because these accounts treat the client's account as material to interpret rather than as a report to be audited, so an inaccuracy damages a reading without destroying the theory. The fourth option fails because reciprocal determinism adds a direction of influence that reward alone cannot express, and an approach that reduces both to reward has removed the disagreement rather than resolved it.
questions.hint: Ask which claims are about what an approach explains, and which are about the evidence it accepts.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: Types Against Dimensions
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a typological classification from a dimensional one
questions.stem: One classification sorts people into kinds, placing each person on one side of a boundary. Another scores every person on every dimension, so a person can sit at the top on one and near the middle on another. What does the second way of organising buy?

options.text: It lets a person be described in several respects at once, and it turns a class membership into a position on a measured scale
It lets a person be assigned to one class with fewer borderline decisions, since each scale supplies a single cut point
options.misconception: describes what classes give, while the second scheme is precisely what replaces them

options.text: It removes the need for a comparison group, since a position on a scale can be read against that person alone
options.misconception: believes a position on a scale means something without knowing what the scale runs through

options.text: It guarantees that people who score alike will behave alike, since they now occupy the same place on a scale
options.misconception: reads a shared position on a scale as a shared set of causes behind conduct

questions.explanation: The contrast is between a boundary and a scale, and everything downstream follows from where the boundary sits. A dimensional description allows a person to be described in several respects at once, which a class cannot do, since a member of a class is a member on the one ground the class was built for, and a person who is high on one scale and average on another is a single fact that a class has no way to record. It also converts membership into position, and a position is measured rather than declared, so it can be compared with a reference group and can be tracked over time. The class option fails because the second scheme describes no classes at all, and a cut point is what it replaces. The comparison-group option fails because a position is meaningless without knowing what the scale runs through, since the middle of a scale is a fact about the group that produced it. The guarantee option fails because a position on a scale is a summary, and two people at 80 on it may be at 80 for reasons that have nothing to do with each other.
questions.hint: Ask what a person high on one scale and middling on another looks like to each scheme.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: The Order of a Classical Psychodynamic Interview
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages by which a psychodynamic account reaches a claim
questions.stem: Put these five stages in the order in which a classical psychodynamic interview is said to reach a claim about a client's difficulties.

options.text: The client is invited to say whatever comes to mind about a present difficulty or a current situation
options.misconception: placing the invitation to speak before the material it is meant to produce is out of order

options.text: The client notices and reports the parts of the material that repeat, including reactions to the therapist
options.misconception: naming recurrent themes before there is any material in which they can recur

options.text: The therapist treats a recurring reaction to the therapist as carrying the weight of a reaction to other people
options.misconception: reading a reaction to the therapist as a sign of its own rather than as a repetition elsewhere

options.text: The recurring themes are connected to material from earlier in life that the client has not yet spoken about
options.misconception: proposing the earlier explanation before the repetition that would motivate it has been established

options.text: The therapist offers an interpretation linking earlier material to the present difficulty and asks whether it fits
options.misconception: offering an interpretation before the pattern it is meant to fit has been described

questions.explanation: The order is a chain of dependencies, and each stage needs what the previous one produced. The invitation to speak freely comes first because it is what generates unstructured material, and a search for repetition has nothing to search through without it. Identifying the repetition comes next, since the account's central claim is that something recurs, and recurrence is a property of material rather than of an intention. The step that treats a reaction to the therapist as carrying the weight of a reaction to other people then converts a repetition inside the sessions into evidence about people outside them, and it is the step that makes the method able to reach the past at all rather than only the room. Connecting the themes to material not yet discussed follows from that conversion, since the material is outside the conversation and has to be brought in as a proposal. The interpretation comes last of all, and it comes last because it is the only stage the client is asked to accept rather than to produce, so putting it early would mean asking for agreement to something the session has not yet earned.
questions.hint: Start with what produces the material, then find what repeats, then reach outside the session, and only then propose.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: The Core Claim of a Trait Account
questions.learningObjective: state what consistency means within a trait account
questions.stem: A trait account holds that people differ from one another in ways that persist across situations, and it claims this is what a personality theory must explain. What does the account take consistency to mean?

options.text: That a person's relative standing on a dimension is roughly preserved across time and across different settings
That a person acts in the same way every time a given situation is met, with no exceptions anywhere in the record
options.misconception: demands exception-free identical behaviour, which no trait account actually requires

options.text: That the traits a person holds are settled for life and cannot be altered at all by later experience
options.misconception: turns a measured and revisable disposition into something fixed for life

options.text: That people who share a trait also share its causes, so grouping by trait automatically groups by history
options.misconception: believes two people at the same score arrived there by the same history

questions.explanation: A trait account is usually criticised for a consistency claim stronger than it needs, and the criticism lands because the claim is often stated too strongly. What the account needs is order to be roughly preserved, that a person who is high relative to others on a dimension in one occasion and setting is still relatively high later, because that is the property that makes the score worth having. Act-level identity would be a much stronger claim and is not made, since the whole difficulty of the field is how much a person's behaviour moves with a setting. The exception-free option fails because nobody claims it and the claim would be self-defeating, since any departure would then refute the trait. The fixed-forever option fails because traits are measured, and a measure that cannot change would not need repeating. The shared-causes option fails because grouping by trait is a description and says nothing about who got the trait from whom, and two people at the same score may have arrived there by different histories.
questions.hint: Ask whether consistency is a claim about a person's behaviour or about their position among other people.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: One Person Across Three Settings
questions.learningObjective: handle a consistency finding as an open question in the person-situation debate
questions.stem: A supervisor who has watched a worker for two years rates her dependable, while two colleagues rate the same worker lively in one setting and guarded in another. How should this be handled in the argument over whether traits predict conduct?

options.text: As a question left open for research, since how consistent conduct is below the level of the closest observers is what the argument turns on
As disproof of traits, since three raters disagreeing about a person shows the disposition never existed to be measured
options.misconception: takes ordinary disagreement among imperfect observers as a refutation of the construct

options.text: As proof of traits, since one rater's stability across two years must reflect a real and durable disposition
options.misconception: promotes a single rater's steadiness to proof while ignoring a narrow sample of occasions

options.text: As a failure of raters, since the best-informed rating should simply replace the two less informed ones
options.misconception: proposes discarding ratings by informant seniority rather than treating them as different samples

questions.explanation: The case is constructed to sit exactly where the argument is unsettled, and the useful move is to say which quantity the disagreement bears on. It bears on average consistency, since the supervisor's steadiness and the colleagues' variation are observations of the same person under different arrangements of observer and setting, and neither settles the general question of how far conduct departs from a trait. This is one of the places in personality where a confident answer is a sign of a badly posed item, because the size of the consistency actually observed has been contested for years and the dispute concerns method as much as result. The disproof option fails because disagreement among observers is the normal condition of any measure that is not perfectly reliable, and a trait claim has never required unanimity. The proof option fails because one rater's stability can come from a narrow sampling of occasions, and a single rater's consistency is weaker evidence than the field's own reliability. The rater-failure option fails because discarding ratings by informant seniority discards information, and the interesting possibility is that the observers sampled different behaviour rather than that some of them are simply wrong.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity the disagreement actually measures, and whether that quantity settles the wider argument.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: The Lexical Hypothesis
questions.learningObjective: state the argument for building traits out of a language's character words
questions.stem: A lexical approach starts from the words a language has for character and builds the trait structure out of them. What is the argument for choosing that starting point?

options.text: That the distinctions a language finds worth making about character are the ones its speakers have found necessary to make in practice
That these words were coined by researchers, so their content reflects the science that produced them rather than usage
options.misconception: credits psychology with inventing the vocabulary whose origins it relies on

options.text: That every character word maps cleanly onto one trait, so the number of words fixes the number of traits
options.misconception: assumes a one-to-one word-to-trait mapping that the whole method exists to remove

options.text: That the words have been stable for centuries, so a modern reader can safely take their present meaning as the original
options.misconception: assumes unchanged meaning across centuries as though the lexicon were fixed

questions.explanation: The lexical strategy rests on a functional claim about language rather than on a claim about experts, and the claim is that a distinction survives in everyday speech because people keep needing to make it. Words for character are therefore treated as a record of practical attention, and any structure the words show is a structure the language has already found useful for getting along with other people. The researchers option fails because most character words long predate the science, and the argument works precisely because the source is not the discipline. The one-word-one-trait option fails because the whole procedure exists because that mapping is false, since synonyms, metaphors and evaluative terms overlap heavily and clustering is what collapses them. The stability option fails because meaning moves even where usage appears steady, and a lexicon method has to be redone when a language changes rather than inherited unchanged from a century back.
questions.hint: Ask what is being assumed about why certain words about character exist at all.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: A Lexicon Study That Split in Two Directions
questions.learningObjective: read a disagreement about the number of trait factors as methodological
questions.stem: A study pools trait adjectives from many sources and reports sixteen broad factors; a later analysis of the same word pool reports five. The disagreement is about what counts as a distinct trait. How should it be read?

options.text: As a methodological dispute about how many dimensions there are, since the count depends on the word pool and the analytic decisions
As a finding of sixteen traits that the later work has now corrected, so the earlier figure is simply out of date
options.misconception: treats a disputed factor count as a settled measurement later shown to be wrong

options.text: As evidence that trait words are unusable, since two competent analyses of one list cannot both be right
options.misconception: concludes from a disagreement about granularity that the descriptors themselves are void

options.text: As a cultural difference, since the two analyses were run in different countries and used different words
options.misconception: invents two national word pools for an argument the vignette reports as one pool

questions.explanation: Two analyses of one word pool can differ in the number of factors they report without either of them being mistaken, and the reason is that the count is partly an output of choices rather than a reading off a property of the words. A larger word pool with more specific terms supports finer factors, a decision about what counts as a distinct descriptor changes the pool, and the method of extracting structure can return different numbers from the same input. So the honest statement is about the state of the question rather than about how many traits people have. The corrected-count option fails because nothing about the later figure establishes it as the true number, and it too rests on a pool and a method. The unusable-words option fails because disagreement about granularity is exactly what a factor analysis is for, since a hierarchy of broad and narrow factors is a coherent structure rather than a failure. The cultural option fails because the vignette describes one pool of words analysed twice, so a difference in national vocabulary cannot be what separated the two results.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two analyses shared the same inputs, and where in the procedure the count could be decided.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: Reading a Table of Factor Loadings
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a cross-loading item in a reported factor solution
questions.stem: A factor analysis of six trait items reports three factors. Kindly loads 0.82, 0.07 and 0.05; Punctual loads 0.07, 0.85 and 0.19; Curious loads 0.09, 0.14 and 0.73; Traditional, written in reverse, loads 0.05, 0.62 and -0.55. Which item is the trouble?

options.text: Traditional, since its two largest loadings are of similar size and it therefore belongs clearly to neither factor
Kindly, since a loading of 0.82 is by itself too slight to anchor a factor of its own
options.misconception: believes a large single loading on its own factor is a weakness rather than a clean anchor

options.text: Curious, because an item must load negatively on a factor before it can be treated as written in reverse
options.misconception: believes a negative sign is a requirement for reverse-wording an item

options.text: Punctual, since an item has to load on every factor in turn before it counts as part of the structure
options.misconception: sets a requirement that items must load on all factors, which is a nuisance factor not a trait

questions.explanation: What makes an item's contribution to a solution is the gap between its own factor and the next largest, not the size of the largest on its own. Traditional has 0.62 on the second factor and -0.55 on the third, so the two are within a few hundredths of each other and the item has no clear home, and the shared variance of 0.62 squared plus 0.55 squared is under two thirds, which means the two factors together still leave a third of the item unexplained. A solution like that is one in which the item should probably be dropped or reworded, since keeping it forces a decision about which factor it belongs to that the data do not support. The Kindly option fails because a loading of 0.82 on its own factor against near zero on the other two is exactly what a defining item looks like, and its shared variance is the highest in the table. The Curious option fails because a negative sign is a matter of how the item was worded and of the sign convention chosen for the factor, and it says nothing about whether the item anchors a factor. The Punctual option fails because an item belongs to a structure by loading on one factor clearly, since loading on everything is what a general nuisance factor looks like rather than a requirement.
questions.hint: Compare each item's largest loading with its second largest, and compute the shared variance.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: Normative Against Ipsative Scoring
questions.learningObjective: state what a forced-choice format is designed to control
questions.stem: One questionnaire asks a respondent to rate how well each of twenty statements describes them. Another asks the respondent to pick which of four statements in each block describes them best, with the four drawn from different scales. What does the second design do?

options.text: It blocks a general tendency to pick the same kind of option, since a block's flattering alternatives are spread across scales
It stops the respondent reading the items as a set, because the blocks are presented in a fixed working order
options.misconception: credits a fixed presentation order with controlling agreement across scales

options.text: It removes any need to remember how one behaved a year ago, because no question about past behaviour is asked
options.misconception: claims the format solves a recall problem that no version of these items raises

options.text: It rules out comparing one person with a norm group, since the total across the scales is fixed by construction
options.misconception: describes a limitation of the format as though the format were designed to prevent comparison

questions.explanation: A forced-choice block exists for one purpose, and it is worth naming precisely, because the cost it imposes is real. Inside a block the desirable statements are distributed across the scales, so a respondent who wants to make a flattering choice has to give up as much on one scale as they gain on another, and a general tendency to agree or to answer agreeably is therefore largely cancelled. What the respondent's total on a scale now means is a preference within their own profile, which is why such a profile is good for ranking a person against themselves and poor as a basis for comparison with others. The ordering option fails because presenting blocks in a fixed order may be convenient and says nothing about agreement tendencies, and the format would be identical under a randomised order. The recall option fails because no version of these items asks about past behaviour, so removing recall cannot be what it is for. The comparison option fails because the fixed total is a limitation of the format rather than a prevention, and it is exactly why normed comparisons become awkward rather than impossible.
questions.hint: Ask what a respondent could do freely in a simple rating, and what a block denies them.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: An Internal Consistency Figure from Four Items
questions.learningObjective: compute an internal consistency coefficient from item and total standard deviations
questions.stem: A four-item scale has item standard deviations of 4, 5, 4 and 3, and the standard deviation of its total score is 10. Using the usual internal-consistency formula, what coefficient do you get?
questions.explanation: The formula is the number of items over one less than the number of items, multiplied by one minus the sum of the item variances over the variance of the total. Here the item variances are 16, 25, 16 and 9, which sum to 66, and the total variance is 100, so the bracket is one minus 0.66, which is 0.34, and four thirds of 0.34 is 0.453. The size of the figure is the substantive part of the answer rather than the arithmetic, because a coefficient this low says the four items are not asking one question, and the reason is visible in the inputs: the total is barely more spread out than the individual items, which happens when the items do not move together. It is also worth remembering that this coefficient depends on the number of items, so a short scale is penalised and the figure could rise with more items that tap the same thing.
questions.hint: Square each item deviation, add them, then use the bracket one minus that sum over the squared total deviation.

questions.stem: A personality questionnaire is given to the same forty people twice, four weeks apart, and the correlation between the two sets of scores is 0.62. What does that figure leave open?

options.text: Whether the shortfall comes from an instrument that is noisy or from real change in the people, since either would produce this figure
Whether the instrument measures personality at all, since a coefficient above zero has already established the answer
options.misconception: believes a coefficient above zero already settles what the score means

options.text: Whether the two sittings measured the same construct, since a correlation cannot compare what two variables mean
options.misconception: looks to a retest coefficient for an answer about what the items actually ask

options.text: Whether the second sitting was administered worse, since a lower second figure always indicates poorer administration
options.misconception: insists on a single cause for a second set of scores that sits lower than the first

questions.explanation: A retest coefficient is the product of two things that are hard to tell apart from the number alone, which is why the same figure can be read in two directions. It is attenuated both by the unreliability of the instrument, since some of the spread in each sitting is error, and by whatever really happened in the four weeks, including mood, season, illness and the ordinary movement of a person's circumstances. A figure of 0.62 is entirely compatible with an instrument of high reliability measuring something that genuinely shifted, and it is equally compatible with a stable person and a noisy instrument. The measures option fails because a coefficient above zero shows only that the two sittings are not independent, and an item that reliably measures nothing but the day of the week also achieves that. The construct option fails because comparing what two variables mean is a question about the design and the items, and a retest figure is not the place to look for it. The administration option fails because a worse second sitting is only one of several reasons a second set of scores could sit lower, and nothing in the figure identifies which reason applies.
questions.hint: Ask what two different situations would each produce the same pair of sittings.

questions.stem: Six people are ranked on conscientiousness in session one and again three months later. The ranks are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and then 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6. First work out the sum of the squared rank differences, then the rank correlation.

The squared differences are 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, summing to 4, and the rank correlation is about 0.44
options.misconception: applies the formula but drops the multiplier that scales total disagreement

options.text: The squared differences are 0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 0, summing to 8, and the rank correlation is about 0.77
options.misconception: reports rank differences of two where the two rankings differ by one

options.text: The squared differences are 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, summing to 6, and the rank correlation is about 0.83
options.misconception: assumes everyone moved a rank even though half held their exact position

questions.explanation: Working person by person gives rank differences of 0, minus 1, 1, minus 1, 1 and 0, and squaring them removes the signs so they are 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, which sums to 4. The 0.77 option fails because it reads a rank difference of 2 where the ranks differ by 1, and with six people such a difference cannot arise. The 0.83 option fails because it treats a difference of 1 as universal when half the people kept their exact position.

questions.topic: Personality: A Table of Reliability Figures
questions.learningObjective: judge which pattern of reliability figures warrants a question
questions.stem: Four instruments are reported with internal consistency and a four-week retest figure. A gives 0.88 and 0.91, B gives 0.61 and 0.24, C gives 0.79 and 0.80, D gives 0.35 and 0.72. Which pattern should a reader pause over?

options.text: Instrument B, because items that agree well with each other while sittings agree poorly are in tension with each other
Instrument A, because a figure as high as that is too steady to be a genuine measurement of a human being
options.misconception: treats high stability as evidence of a fake rather than of a reliable instrument

options.text: Instrument C, because two figures that nearly match tell the reader nothing about the instrument whatever they say
options.misconception: reads a favourable pair of figures as an absence of information

options.text: Instrument D, because both figures can only be high at once if the instrument is not measuring anything at all
options.misconception: believes low item agreement and high stability cannot occur in the same instrument

questions.explanation: The two figures answer different questions, and their combination is what makes a pattern interpretable. Internal consistency asks whether items thought to measure one thing move together, and a retest figure asks whether the whole score reproduces after a short interval. Instrument B pulls these apart, because items that agree well while occasions agree badly suggests either that the items are related but the score is dominated by whatever is happening that week, or that the two sittings differed in a way that has nothing to do with the construct, and either reading is a reason to ask what happened. The A option fails because high stability is what a reliable instrument looks like, and nothing about a person is unrealistic just because the measurement is steady. The C option fails because a good internal figure with a good stability figure is a favourable result and the near-match is a strength rather than an absence of information. The D option fails because low internal consistency with high stability is entirely possible, since a short scale can be reproducible and still be measuring several things at once, and that combination points at the item set rather than at nothingness.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: What a Reliability Figure Is For
questions.learningObjective: state what a reliability coefficient does and does not establish
questions.stem: A report gives one reliability coefficient for a new personality inventory and uses it to present the instrument as trustworthy. What is that coefficient evidence of?

options.text: That the scores hang together, and if a retest figure is also given that they persist; neither says what the scores measure
That the inventory measures personality, since a score that cannot be trusted would not be able to describe anybody
options.misconception: collapses reliability into validity and treats consistent scores as correct ones

options.text: That the inventory anticipates later behaviour, since a consistent score is also a score that predicts outcomes
options.misconception: assumes a self-consistent score must therefore forecast a later outcome

options.text: That the inventory is untouched by what participants were told, since any such effect would surface as noise
options.misconception: expects a systematic effect of instructions to show up as random error

questions.explanation: Reliability and validity are separate properties and a single coefficient belongs to the first, and the confusion between them is the commonest way a new instrument is oversold. A reliability figure says that some part of the difference between two people's scores is not error in the scoring or the occasion, and a retest figure adds that some of it survives a short interval. What the score varies with is a different question, answered by comparing the score with something outside the instrument or by reasoning about what the items ask. The measurement option fails because a scale can be perfectly reliable while measuring a preference for one of two response formats, and the number would be no lower for that. The prediction option fails because anticipating an outcome is a criterion claim about a relationship that has to be demonstrated with data, and no amount of internal consistency supplies it. The instruction option fails because an influence of what participants were told would show up as a systematic difference between conditions rather than as noise, and noise is what reliability is about.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two big questions a coefficient about hang-together can answer, and which it leaves open.

questions.topic: Personality: What a Projective Technique Is Designed to Obtain
questions.learningObjective: state what a projective technique is built to sample
questions.stem: One personality instrument gives a fixed set of statements to be rated yes or no. Another shows an ambiguous picture and asks the respondent to say what is going on, then scores the themes in the answer. What is the second instrument built to obtain?

options.text: A sample of the respondent's own way of construing an ambiguous situation, which is hard to fake because no right answer exists to give
An accurate count of the respondent's traits, since a scored story lists each trait the respondent actually has
options.misconception: confuses a thematic reading with a direct inventory of traits

options.text: A diagnosis of a disorder, since the themes in a story reveal which condition the respondent currently meets
options.misconception: believes a scored story is a diagnostic instrument on its own

options.text: A reading of early childhood, since a story about a scene is evidence about the respondent's own childhood
options.misconception: treats a projected story as a report about what really happened to the respondent

questions.explanation: A projective technique is built around the idea that a person's construal of an ambiguous stimulus is itself the datum, and everything else about the design follows from that. The count option fails because a story contains a handful of themes and not a set of measured scores, and the traits named in a story are a small selected sample rather than a profile. The diagnosis option fails because a theme is not a symptom, and diagnosis requires a set of necessary features, duration and impairment rather than a narrative resemblance. The childhood option fails because the events described belong to the stimulus's world, and the interest is in what the respondent put there, which makes the technique a sample of construal and not an archive of biography.

Recording who is arguing and who is loud, since the structure of the story can be checked against the picture

questions.topic: Personality: Nomothetic Against Idiographic
questions.learningObjective: state what a case-based account gives up by not generalising
questions.stem: One programme looks for general laws about average differences between people on measured traits. Another builds a detailed account of why one person is as they are. What does the second programme give up by going case by case?

options.text: A claim that will hold for people in general, since its conclusions are drawn from one case and cannot be sampled
Access to the person's own sense of their situation, since a case account has to work from the outside
options.misconception: believes a case account is obliged to take the outside view of the person

options.text: Any record of how the person compares with others, since a single case contains no comparison whatever
options.misconception: assumes a single case is devoid of comparison and ignores comparison over time

options.text: The chance to revise the account as the case develops, since a general law cannot be amended by one history
options.misconception: believes case accounts are fixed and general laws are the revisable ones

questions.explanation: The trade is between reach and depth, and it is worth stating precisely because both programmes answer questions the other cannot. A single case can be followed in a way no sample can be, since the person's own account, the sequence of events and the changes over time are all available, and what it cannot deliver is a claim about people in general, because one case cannot be sampled and any statement drawn from it may be a feature of that person or that moment. The outside option fails because a case account in this tradition works with the person's own sense of their situation, and that is its main source of material. The comparison option fails because a single case is not devoid of comparison, since the person can be compared with their own earlier state or with the record, and longitudinal comparison is often its strongest feature. The revision option fails because case accounts are revised constantly, and a general law may also be amended by a striking case, so this is a difference in emphasis rather than a limitation in one direction only.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: Reading a Low Retest Figure on a Projective Technique
questions.learningObjective: explain why a stability figure means different things for structured and projective scoring
questions.stem: A projective technique is given to the same people a fortnight apart and each set of stories is scored by a different judge, and the agreement between the two sittings is low. Explain why that is harder to interpret here than for a fixed-item inventory.

answer.exemplar: The result is harder to interpret because the two sittings differ in more than one thing, and a fixed-item design is arranged so that only the person can change while a projective design is not. With a list of statements, the words are identical on both occasions, so a difference between the two score sets has to come from the person, from the timing, or from the scoring, and those can be told apart by holding two of the three still. With an ambiguous card, the person's current construal, the card, the judge and the rules for recognising a theme have all been allowed to differ, so a low figure is close to the arithmetic consequence of that much freedom rather than a surprising finding. The useful response is therefore to ask which of the four things was free to vary rather than to conclude that the person is inconsistent. A design that would sharpen the point holds the card set, the scoring rules and the judge constant and varies only the interval, because then the only remaining source of disagreement is the construal on the two days, and any longer gap or any change of card can be tested separately. Evidence against the idea that people impose their own structure would be a variant in which the scoring depends little on which story a person tells, since if the ambiguity is doing the work a clearer prompt ought to reduce disagreement. What the low figure does not establish is that nothing is being measured, because a measure of an ongoing construction will be unstable whenever the construction is unstable, and that is a fact about the construct as much as about the instrument.

questions.explanation: The answer has to identify what was allowed to differ between the two sittings, explain why that is more than the person, and propose a design that holds everything but the construal still. It should also say what the low figure does not show, since instability in a score is expected whenever the thing measured is an interpretation, and treating that as a refutation mistakes a property of the construct for a defect of the measure.
questions.hint: Ask what was identical on the two occasions, and whether the person was the only thing that could have changed.

A response that differs between sittings may reflect the ambiguity of the card rather than a change in the person
Because there is no right answer to an ambiguous card, the resulting score reflects the examiner's expectations more reliably than the respondent's mind

questions.learningObjective: compute an agreement figure corrected for the chance level in the design
questions.stem: Two judges each classify 100 projective stories as showing conflict or not. Both say yes on 62, both say no on 28, judge one says yes alone on 5 and judge two says yes alone on 5. What should be reported?

options.text: Neither figure, since two judges cannot be compared at all until a third judge has adjudicated between them
options.misconception: demands a third judge before any agreement figure may be computed

questions.topic: Personality: Two Readings of a Faking Problem
questions.learningObjective: identify the two available readings of a context-dependent score change
questions.stem: Reviewers note that applicants score higher on a personality inventory when told it is being used to screen them for a job than when the same people answer in an unrelated study. What are the two available readings?

options.text: That people adjust their answers toward what they think will look good, and that the score is therefore partly a report of what a situation rewards
That the inventory is unusable, so that any change of this kind amounts to proof that the underlying traits are not real
options.misconception: turns a finding about response style into a refutation of the traits

options.text: That the underlying traits are themselves unstable, so a change of score is direct evidence that the personality changed
options.misconception: reads a difference between settings as a change in the person, who is held constant

options.text: That the applicants simply remembered their earlier answers, since both sittings used identical item wording
options.misconception: blames recall of an earlier sitting for a difference created by a new one

questions.explanation: The pattern is a well-known problem and the useful response is to hold both readings at once, because each is a real contribution to what a score means. On the first, people are reporting a strategy rather than a disposition, and a setting that rewards a particular answer will produce it, which makes the score partly a measure of the stakes. On the second, and this is the half usually left out, the same person in a setting with no consequences has produced a lower score, and that lower score is evidence about something too. Neither half is a refutation of anything, since the first describes an interaction and the second describes what happens when it is absent. The unusable option fails because a response that shifts with the stakes is a normal property of self-report, not a verdict on the traits, and instruments that survive this critique do so by measuring something other than what a respondent would like to claim. The instability option fails because nothing in the pattern shows the person changed, since the whole design contrasts settings and holds the person constant. The memory option fails because nothing in the design invites recall of an earlier sitting, and identical wording is a constant rather than a cause of difference.
questions.hint: Ask what changed between the two sittings, and then ask what the lower score in the second setting is evidence about.

questions.learningObjective: state what the preference for confirming self-beliefs implies about negative feedback
questions.stem: People given negative feedback about a trait they score high on feel worse about themselves than people given the same feedback about a trait they score low on. What account does that pattern support?

options.text: That people would rather have their existing self-beliefs confirmed even when the confirmation is unflattering than have them corrected
That people take any criticism badly, with no regard to which trait it concerns or how they scored on it
options.misconception: ignores the trait on which the person actually scored

options.text: That negative feedback lowers the self-concept whichever trait it concerns, so the effect is about the message
options.misconception: predicts the same reaction regardless of which trait the feedback concerns

options.text: That people score high on the traits that most threaten them, since the discomfort comes from the trait rather than the verdict
options.misconception: explains the reaction by which trait was threatening rather than by the standing of the belief

questions.explanation: The interesting part of the pattern is that the same bad news hurts more in one case than the other, and the account that explains it is about the standing of a belief rather than about the message. A person who already sees themselves as conscientious is being asked to give up a self-belief, and giving one up is costly in a way that hearing unwelcome news about a trait is not, so the unflattering confirmation lands harder. options.text: Each resulting factor is given a name and treated as a candidate dimension of personality

questions.learningObjective: design a test of whether a self-report predicts beyond a behavioural record
questions.stem: A team holds a behavioural record of how consistently people attend a scheduled task and a self-report of conscientiousness from the same people. Design a study that could say whether the self-report predicts anything the record misses.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: A Trait and a State in One Person
questions.learningObjective: explain what trait and state accounts each contribute to one case
questions.stem: A person is described as calm in most settings and loses their temper twice a week in one particular setting. Explain what a trait account and a state account each contribute, and what neither can settle.

answer.exemplar: The trait account contributes the cross-situational part of the description and the observation that most settings produce the same response, which is what a disposition claim is made of and what lets a person be described as calm at all rather than merely calm once. It also predicts where to look next, since a disposition should show up wherever the demands are similar, and the exception marks a setting where something other than the disposition is doing the work. The state account contributes the local account, since a temper twice a week in one setting is a state in that setting and the fact that it recurs makes it something about the setting rather than a bad moment, which points at what happens there, who is present, or what the person is trying to achieve. Neither settles which of the two explains the difference, because the case as described does not say whether the calm is a disposition that the setting overrides or a set of separate states that happen to resemble one another, and that is the point at which the two accounts make different predictions. A design that would help holds the person constant and varies the setting, recording the response in each across enough occasions to see whether the pattern follows the person or the setting, and then tests the same person in the difficult setting with one element of it removed. What neither account can do is state which of them is true, since a disposition and a repeating state can produce the same table, and a trait account is in any case a summary rather than an explanation of why the summary holds.

questions.explanation: The answer has to give each account the part of the description it is good at, say why the case as stated does not decide between them, and propose a way to vary the setting while holding the person fixed. It should also note that a trait is a summary and so is not itself a mechanism, which is why settling between the two accounts would still leave a question about why the person is calm in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the description each account explains, and what a design would have to vary to tell them apart.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: Turning the Consistency Debate Into a Research Question
questions.learningObjective: design an estimate of cross-situational consistency that bears on the debate
questions.stem: An investigation wants to estimate how consistent a trait is across settings in a way that could bear on the person-situation argument. Explain what it must control and what it must report.

answer.exemplar: The first requirement is that the same people be observed in more than one setting, because a study in which each person is observed once cannot produce a consistency figure at all, and the second is that the settings differ in the demands they place on the trait rather than in how convenient they are to arrange. Several settings are needed rather than two, since with two occasions a person who is consistent in one direction and inconsistent in the other is indistinguishable from one who is simply unreliable, and the pattern of agreements and disagreements across pairs of settings is what separates the two. Reliability of the occasion measure has to be estimated rather than assumed, since a single rating of a person's trait carries error and that error alone produces a figure below one, so the estimate should be of consistency in the trait rather than of agreement of ratings. The settings should be sampled rather than chosen for convenience, and the number of occasions per person should be the same throughout, since an uneven number of opportunities makes a person's total agreement uninterpretable. Report the design's reliability alongside the consistency figure, because a figure near zero is expected when the measure is noisy, and report it separately for each pair of settings, since an average across settings hides whether a trait is stable in some pairs and not others. The figure should be reported as a rank or a correlation with an interval, since a single coefficient from a modest number of occasions looks more precise than it is, and the debate is sensitive to the difference between a small number and a moderate one rather than to a decimal place. What the investigation cannot deliver is a verdict on the accounts, since consistency above chance is compatible with a disposition, and its size depends on which settings were sampled and on how much of the difference between settings the design allowed to matter.

questions.explanation: The answer has to insist on several occasions per person, on sampling settings rather than picking convenient ones, and on reporting the reliability of the occasion measure beside the consistency figure. It should also say that the result is a parameter that depends on which settings were sampled, so a single number cannot settle an argument about how much conduct depends on context.
questions.hint: Ask how many occasions each person needs, and what has to be reported alongside the consistency figure.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: One Client, Two Accounts
questions.learningObjective: synthesise what two approaches contribute to one case and where they conflict
questions.stem: A client who is reliably late describes an early memory of a parent who was also always late, and holds that the memory is the reason. Synthesise what a trait account and a psychodynamic account each contribute, and where they conflict.

answer.exemplar: The trait account contributes a description the case can be checked against, since lateness is a countable behaviour and a scale or an observer record can say how consistent it is across contexts and how far back it runs. It also declines to say why, and that limitation is not a gap in the account but the boundary of what a disposition claim is. The psychodynamic account contributes a proposed mechanism rather than a description, in which an expectation formed with an early parent transfers to situations with no such history, and it makes a prediction the trait account does not, namely that the pattern should be tied to the expectation rather than to punctuality as such. The conflict is therefore not between two descriptions of what happened but between a description and an explanation that makes the same prediction in this case, and one case cannot separate them, because a person raised by a late parent who is now late everywhere is exactly what both accounts expect. What would separate them is evidence about the process rather than about the pattern, such as whether the lateness appears in settings where no expectation about lateness has been formed, whether it appears at all where the deadline is enforced by someone else, and whether it changes when the expectation is deliberately altered. The synthesis should also record what the accounts share, which is that a stable pattern is present and worth explaining, and it should treat the client's conviction about the cause as evidence about the case without treating it as evidence for the mechanism, since a person can be right about a pattern and wrong about its source.

The trait account contributes a description in terms the case can be checked against, since lateness is a countable behaviour and a scale or an observer record can say how consistent it is across contexts and how far back it goes. The psychodynamic account contributes a proposed mechanism, since the memory of a late parent offers a reason for the pattern rather than a description of it, and it makes a prediction that a trait account does not, namely that the pattern should show up where the relevant expectation has been formed. The conflict is not between two descriptions but between a description and an explanation that happens to make the same prediction here, and a reader cannot separate them from one case because the pattern of lateness is exactly what both accounts predict in a person raised by a late parent. What would separate them is evidence about the process, such as whether the lateness appears in settings where no expectation about lateness has been formed, and whether it changes when the expectation is altered. The synthesis should also record what both accounts share, which is that a stable pattern is present, and note that the client's conviction about the cause is itself evidence about the case without being evidence for the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask which account is describing a countable pattern, which is proposing a reason, and what evidence would tell them apart.

questions.topic: Personality: Reconciling a Score With a Life
questions.learningObjective: synthesise what a score, a record and an account can each be taken to show
questions.stem: A person scores near the top of a conscientiousness factor, has never held a job longer than four months, and says the work was always unfair. Synthesise what the score, the record and the account can each be taken to show.

answer.exemplar: The three sources are of different kinds and the synthesis has to keep them apart rather than weigh them against one another. The score is a position on a scale produced on one occasion from a fixed item set, so it reports how the person described themselves on that day and it carries whatever the items and the occasion contributed, including any tendency to endorse agreeable statements. The record is a count of how long jobs lasted, and it is a better-measured observation of something a person may be poorly placed to report, but four months of experience in several jobs is a narrow base, and someone who leaves every job quickly gets few opportunities to show sustained performance. The account is the person's own explanation and it is the only one of the three that can report a reason, so it belongs in the synthesis as a claim to be examined rather than as either a description or a distortion. What the three jointly support is a disagreement worth investigating, and the sharpest point is that the two measurable sources are not obviously about the same behaviour, since conscientiousness as it is usually scaled concerns orderliness, persistence about tasks and dutifulness rather than remaining in a job, so a high score and short jobs can be consistent. Second, doubling a coefficient is not free: going from a four-item to an eight-item scale improves the figure far less than going from eight to sixteen, because error falls more slowly than length rises, and that is why a very short scale can be disappointing no matter how good its items are. A figure of 0.90 is respectable and does not say what the scale measures.

The mean says how much the item draws agreement across people and the coefficient says how much people differ from one another on it, and an item endorsed by almost everyone with a coefficient of 0.12 is being endorsed by almost everyone in the same way, so it separates nobody. That group is the problem, and the usual remedies are to reword the item, make it more extreme, or remove it, since a scale made of such items will have a low figure however good it looks. The high-coefficient option fails because a coefficient of 0.74 is a favourable sign and a middling mean says nothing about wording. The low-endorsement option fails because items with low means are common and can be well made, and difficulty is not the same as fault. The wording-direction option fails because a low coefficient is what any item with little between-person variation gives, and there is no evidence here about direction, which would show up as a negative correlation with the scale's other items rather than as a low one.
questions.hint: Read the mean and the coefficient as two separate facts, and ask which group separates nobody.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Personality: A Score Used for a Hiring Decision
questions.learningObjective: state the scope of a criterion validation when a score is used for a decision
questions.stem: A council shortlists applicants using a validated personality inventory, where the validation showed the total predicts completion of a training course with a correlation of 0.31. What is the strongest available claim?

options.text: The score carries information about who finishes training, and using it to select on that basis is a decision about training rather than about job performance
The score is validated for hiring, since the validation was carried out using an applicant sample
options.misconception: confuses the population used with the outcome the figure was obtained against

options.text: Applicants above the midpoint on the total will outperform those below it in the job itself
options.misconception: extends a course-completion figure to on-the-job performance with no new data

options.text: A correlation of 0.31 is too low to be useful, so the council must abandon the score entirely
options.misconception: applies a blanket threshold below which no measure may be used for any decision

questions.explanation: A validation figure belongs to the criterion it was obtained against, and the criterion in the vignette is completing a training course. That is enough to say the total is not empty and that it carries information about who will get through a course, and it is not enough to say anything at all about performance in the job, which is a different outcome that has to be measured and related to the score in its own right. The scope of the claim is the whole point, and getting it wrong in either direction is the standard error here. The hiring option fails because the sample being applicants is not the criterion, and validation attaches to the outcome rather than to the population, though the population also matters for how far the figure travels. The outperforms option fails by extending a course-completion figure to on-the-job performance without any data. The too-low option fails because no criterion demands a large correlation before a measure may be used, and a useful decision can rest on a small association, though the cost of a wrong decision and the base rate then have to enter the argument.
questions.hint: Ask which outcome the figure was obtained against, and what it says about a different one.
